songs.title: First look at the data
songs.desc: Show name and energy for the first five songs by ascending id. Return those two columns in that order.
songs.starter:
SELECT name, energy
FROM songs
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5;
songs.answer:
SELECT name, energy
FROM songs
ORDER BY id ASC
LIMIT 5;
songs.hint: Select the columns, order by id, then use LIMIT 5.
songs.explain: SELECT returns the two requested fields. Sorting by id identifies which five songs to return.

songs.title: Apply three conditions
songs.desc: Find songs with danceability, energy and valence all greater than 0.6. Return only name. Row order is optional.
songs.answer:
SELECT name
FROM songs
WHERE danceability > 0.6
  AND energy > 0.6
  AND valence > 0.6;
songs.hint: All three conditions must hold. Use AND.
songs.explain: AND requires all three conditions to be true. The complete course database returns 23 songs.

songs.title: Join songs to artists
songs.desc: Find all songs by looking up Drake by artist name. Return only the song name. Row order is optional.
songs.starter:
SELECT s.name
FROM songs AS s
-- Join songs to artists here
songs.answer:
SELECT s.name
FROM songs AS s
JOIN artists AS a ON s.artist_id = a.id
WHERE a.name = 'Drake';
songs.hint: Match songs.artist_id to artists.id. The artist name is in artists.name.
songs.explain: Join the tables by ID and filter by artist name. An equivalent subquery also works.

songs.title: Find the most danceable songs
songs.desc: Return name and danceability for the five highest-scoring songs. Sort by danceability descending, then id ascending for ties.
songs.answer: SELECT name, danceability FROM songs ORDER BY danceability DESC, id LIMIT 5;
songs.explain: The secondary sort makes the top five reproducible.

songs.title: Average energy across the song list
songs.desc: Return the average energy of all songs as one number. Keep the full precision.
songs.hint: Use AVG on the energy column.
songs.explain: Each song contributes one energy value to the mean.

songs.title: Count songs by artist
songs.desc: Return artist name and song count for every artist represented in the song list. Sort by count descending, artist name ascending, then artist ID ascending.
songs.starter: SELECT a.name FROM artists AS a
songs.answer: SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS SongCount FROM songs s JOIN artists a ON s.artist_id=a.id GROUP BY a.id,a.name ORDER BY SongCount DESC,a.name,a.id;
songs.hint: Join artist ID to song artist_id. Group by artist ID and name.
songs.explain: The artist ID keeps separate artists distinct even if names match.

songs.title: List the full song catalogue
songs.desc: Return name and energy for every song. Row order is optional.
songs.hint: Select two columns and keep all rows.
songs.explain: This query returns both requested columns for all 100 songs.

songs.title: Sort songs by tempo
songs.desc: Return song names from fastest to slowest by tempo. Break ties by id ascending.
songs.answer: SELECT name FROM songs ORDER BY tempo DESC, id;
songs.hint: You can sort by a column without returning it.
songs.explain: Tempo supplies the ranking, and id makes ties deterministic.

songs.title: Find the three longest songs
songs.desc: Return only the names of the three longest songs. Sort by duration_ms descending, then id ascending.
songs.answer: SELECT name FROM songs ORDER BY duration_ms DESC, id LIMIT 3;
songs.hint: Sort by duration before taking the first three.
songs.explain: LIMIT keeps the top three after the descending sort.

songs.title: Calculate average tempo
songs.desc: Return the average tempo of all songs as one number. Keep full precision.
songs.hint: AVG combines the tempo values into one result.
songs.explain: The average uses the full song catalogue.

songs.title: Find average energy for Post Malone
songs.desc: Find Post Malone by artist name and return the average energy of his songs. Keep full precision.
songs.answer: SELECT AVG(s.energy) FROM songs s JOIN artists a ON a.id=s.artist_id WHERE a.name='Post Malone';
songs.hint: Join on the artist ID, then filter the artist name.
songs.explain: The artist name determines which songs enter the average.

songs.title: Find songs with featured artists
songs.desc: Return the names of songs containing feat. anywhere in the name. Row order is optional.
songs.answer: SELECT name FROM songs WHERE name LIKE '%feat.%';
songs.explain: The percent signs allow any text on either side of feat.

chinook.title: Count invoices above $20
chinook.desc: How many invoices have a Total strictly greater than 20? Return one number in one column.
chinook.hint: Filter by Total, then use COUNT(*).
chinook.explain: COUNT(*) counts the invoices that meet the condition. The strict threshold excludes invoices of exactly $20.

chinook.title: Invoice revenue without double-counting
chinook.desc: Find the total value of all invoices. Count each invoice once and return one number.
chinook.starter:
SELECT SUM(i.Total)
FROM Invoice AS i
JOIN InvoiceLine AS il
  ON il.InvoiceId = i.InvoiceId;
chinook.answer:
SELECT SUM(Total) AS InvoiceValue
FROM Invoice;
chinook.hint: An invoice can have multiple lines. What happens to i.Total when you join to InvoiceLine?
chinook.explain: Invoice contains one row per invoice. Joining to InvoiceLine repeats the invoice totals. The correct total is $2,328.60.

chinook.title: Rank countries by invoice value
chinook.desc: Return BillingCountry and the sum of Total per country. Sort by total descending, then by country alphabetically for ties.
chinook.starter:
SELECT BillingCountry, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
FROM Invoice
-- Add grouping and ordering
chinook.answer:
SELECT BillingCountry, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry
ORDER BY Revenue DESC, BillingCountry ASC;
chinook.hint: Use GROUP BY to group invoices by country and ORDER BY SUM(Total) DESC to rank them.
chinook.explain: Grouping and summing gives one row per country. The secondary sort breaks ties consistently.

chinook.title: Summarise invoice values by customer
chinook.desc: Return CustomerId and total invoice value for each customer with invoices. Use one row per customer. Row order is optional.
chinook.answer: SELECT CustomerId, SUM(Total) FROM Invoice GROUP BY CustomerId;
chinook.hint: Invoice already has one row per invoice. Group by CustomerId.
chinook.explain: This measures billed value by customer without repeating invoice totals.

chinook.title: Find the five most recent invoices
chinook.desc: Return InvoiceId, InvoiceDate and Total for the five most recent invoices. Sort by date descending and InvoiceId descending for ties.
chinook.starter: SELECT InvoiceId, InvoiceDate, Total FROM Invoice
chinook.answer: SELECT InvoiceId, InvoiceDate, Total FROM Invoice ORDER BY InvoiceDate DESC, InvoiceId DESC LIMIT 5;
chinook.hint: Use ORDER BY on both fields before LIMIT.
chinook.explain: InvoiceId determines which invoice comes first on a shared date.

chinook.title: Count unique billed customers by country
chinook.desc: Return BillingCountry and the number of distinct CustomerId values for each country. Row order is optional.
chinook.answer: SELECT BillingCountry, COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerId) FROM Invoice GROUP BY BillingCountry;
chinook.hint: Count distinct customers within each billing country.
chinook.explain: The unit being counted is the customer ID, so repeat invoices do not inflate the count.

employees.title: Combine first and last names
employees.desc: Combine FirstName in column B and LastName in column C with one space. Start in row 2 and fill down for all 597 employees.
employees.hint: Use & to join the text and put the space in double quotes.
employees.explain: The first result is Carl Rodriguez. Relative references adjust as you fill the formula down.

employees.title: Extract the plant ID
employees.desc: Extract PlantID from EmployeeCode in column A. The plant ID has one or two digits after the hyphen and before M, Mo, W or We. Return a number.
employees.hint: Use FIND to locate the hyphen. Subtract its position and the suffix length from the total length. Mo and We have two characters. M and W have one. Use VALUE to return a number.
employees.explain: Japan177-3Mo returns 3. Using FIND lets the formula handle country and employee codes of varying lengths.

employees.title: Classify monthly and weekly codes
employees.desc: Return "Monthly" for codes ending in M or Mo and "Weekly" for W or We. Use EmployeeCode in column A and fill down.
employees.hint: RIGHT(A2,1) returns o for a code ending in Mo. Use OR to test for both M and Mo.
employees.explain: The dataset contains 181 Mo codes, 158 M codes and 258 W codes. We is also a valid suffix. A production system should flag invalid codes separately.

employees.title: Extract the code before the hyphen
employees.desc: Return the portion of EmployeeCode before its first hyphen. Use column A and fill down.
employees.hint: Use FIND to locate the hyphen, then subtract one.
employees.explain: Japan177-3Mo becomes Japan177. The extracted prefix can vary in length.

employees.title: Build uppercase employee initials
employees.desc: Return two uppercase initials, using the first character of FirstName in B and LastName in C. Use no space. Fill down.
employees.hint: Use LEFT for each initial and UPPER for the combined result.
employees.explain: Carl Rodriguez becomes CR. Initials are useful labels, but multiple employees can share them.

employees.title: Measure employee code length
employees.desc: Count the characters in each EmployeeCode in column A, including the hyphen and pay-frequency suffix. Fill down.
employees.hint: LEN counts all characters in a cell.
employees.explain: The lengths help you see why a single fixed-width extraction can fail.

payroll.title: Calculate gross pay per row
payroll.desc: Calculate gross pay per payroll row by adding Reg_Pay in column C and OT_Pay in column D. Start in row 2.
payroll.hint: Gross pay here is the sum of regular and overtime pay.
payroll.explain: Each row represents a payroll allocation. Keep all 4,981 rows.

payroll.title: Calculate total hours
payroll.desc: Calculate total regular and overtime hours across all 4,981 rows. Reg_Hrs is in column A and OT_Hrs in column B. Use rows 2 through 4,982 and return one total.
payroll.hint: Include regular and overtime hours. You can sum the entire range A2:B4982.
payroll.explain: The total is 32,878.75 hours. AVERAGE would give the hours per row.

payroll.title: Calculate gross pay per hour
payroll.desc: Divide total gross pay by total hours in the 2015 extract. Columns A and B contain hours. Columns C and D contain pay. Use rows 2 through 4,982 and round to two decimals.
payroll.hint: Include overtime in both totals, then divide total pay by total hours.
payroll.explain: $1,086,734.19 divided by 32,878.75 hours gives $33.05 per hour. Seven rows have pay and zero hours. The total retains their pay amounts, which warrant a closer look before drawing a business conclusion.

payroll.title: Calculate total overtime pay
payroll.desc: Calculate total OT_Pay in column D over rows 2 through 4,982. Return one number.
payroll.explain: This isolates the overtime component of gross pay.

payroll.title: Calculate overtime as a share of hours
payroll.desc: Divide total OT_Hrs in B by total hours in A and B, using rows 2 through 4,982. Return a decimal fraction with full precision.
payroll.hint: Add both hours columns in the denominator.
payroll.explain: The fraction uses all hours. Multiply by 100 only when presenting it as a percentage.

payroll.title: Flag paid rows with zero hours
payroll.desc: Return "Review" when regular plus overtime hours are zero and regular plus overtime pay is nonzero. Otherwise return "OK". Hours are in A and B, pay in C and D. Fill down.
payroll.hint: Test both conditions together with AND.
payroll.explain: The rule flags seven rows for follow-up. A flag alone does not establish a payroll error.
